code.originalText: Six-month review: diagnosis, relapse prevention, movement check, and alcohol

text.paragraph: Six-month review: diagnosis, relapse prevention, movement check, and alcohol. [S]

Mr. van Gogh returns six months after his first visit. He has had no psychotic symptoms for more than four months and no racing ideas since the spring. He takes aripiprazole 10 mg and naltrexone daily. He sleeps seven hours. He is painting every day and preparing work for a small exhibition. He drinks a glass of wine with dinner on some days and none on others. His mood is good. The care coordinator's monthly PHQ-9 calls have been in the low range. He has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm. His hepatitis C antibody from the preventive visit was nonreactive. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1889-07-20; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well; weight 65.4 kg; blood pressure 118/76, pulse 70
AIMS score 0: no abnormal movements of the face, lips, jaw, tongue, limbs, or trunk; no akathisia or rigidity
Euthymic and engaged; organized; no psychotic features

First episode of psychosis with mood features: weeks of very little sleep, intense work and expansive plans, then acute confusion, hallucinations and suspiciousness with self-injury, and low mood since discharge. Diagnosis provisional; differential: bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, brief psychotic or schizophreniform disorder, alcohol withdrawal delirium or alcohol-induced psychotic disorder, and psychosis related to focal epilepsy. Synthetic modern episode linked to his documented first crisis
S — Synthetic modern coding of the documented first crisis. Unspecified psychosis is coded because the cause is not yet established; the retrospective diagnoses stay in the claims.
Alcohol use disorder, moderate (heavy daily wine and anise spirits before the episode); synthetic modern episode linked to his documented heavy drinking
S — Synthetic modern coding of the documented drinking and its retrospective interpretation.
Self-injury to the left ear during the acute confusional episode, without suicidal intent; wound healed after surgical care in hospital
S — Synthetic modern coding of the documented injury; no detail of the injury is recorded.
Akathisia from aripiprazole, two weeks after the dose was increased to 15 mg; treated by returning to 10 mg and short-term propranolol; resolved
S — Synthetic medication side effect; not a historical claim.

value.displayName: Unspecified psychosis not due to a substance or known physiological condition

list.item:
First episode of psychosis with mood features, provisional diagnosis, in remission (F29). Full remission for more than four months, with no symptoms between, a normal MRI and EEG, and no seizure-like events. This course makes schizophrenia unlikely and leaves bipolar I disorder with psychotic features and a psychosis related to heavy drinking and its sudden withdrawal as the leading possibilities. The diagnosis stays provisional: a manic or depressive episode would point to bipolar disorder, and psychosis without mood change or alcohol would point to a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder. A mood stabilizer would be considered if a mood episode occurs. AIMS score 0. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or self-harm; the safety plan and psychiatric advance directive are current. [S]
Continue aripiprazole 10 mg daily.
Decide with him and Dr. Feld near the one-year mark whether and how slowly to reduce it, with a written relapse plan.
AIMS again in six months; glucose, A1c and lipids yearly.

Alcohol use disorder on naltrexone (F10.20). PEth 16 ng/mL, from 284 at intake: light drinking, as he chose. AST 27, ALT 26 and GGT 36 U/L normal; MCV back to 95 fL. [S]
Continue naltrexone for at least six more months, then review.
Stop thiamine now that drinking is light and meals are regular.

Follow-up: Visits every three months with weight and the PHQ-9. Psychiatry review with Dr. Feld near the one-year mark about the length of antipsychotic treatment. AIMS in six months; glucose, A1c and lipids in a year. Influenza and COVID-19 vaccines in the autumn. [S]
